narrative:
Meridian Actuarial Advisors is a consulting actuarial practice founded in
2014, serving public pension boards, a mid-sized life insurer, and two
multiemployer benefit funds. It is the fastest-growing firm in this
fleet: it starts at six seats and opens five more over nine years,
because that is what a book of work compounding at ten percent a year
actually requires.

Its work carries the discipline of a regulated opinion: precise about
scope, data reliance, and the standards a piece of work is performed
under, plain and undecorated, and careful to separate what the data show
from what was assumed. Between formal deliverables, the actuaries and the
client's staff exchange short emails about data files and assumptions.

Tone is careful and heavily qualified, because an actuary who overstates
a number is exposed. Writing distinguishes measurement from judgment
explicitly: what the data show, what was assumed, and what the actuary
concludes are three different paragraphs. Two staff members share a
surname, and documents that name both should not disambiguate them for
the reader; the firm's own writing treats it as unremarkable, which is
the point.
instructions:
Author every document briefed in `docs`, as JSON matching the deliverable
schema:

  {"schema_id": "orgsmith/authoring-deliverable@1",
   "work_order_id": "wo:author:0009",
   "docs": [{"schema_id": "orgsmith/docir@1", "doc_id": "d:....",
             "blocks": [...]}, ...]}

Block kinds: heading (text, level), paragraph (text), list (items),
table (header, rows), sigblock (signers = person ids from the brief).

Hard rules:
- One DocIR per brief; doc_ids must match the work order exactly.
- Every fact id briefed for a doc MUST appear as a literal placeholder
  {{fact:<id>}} at least once in that doc's text, where <id> is the
  briefed id verbatim including its `f:` prefix (e.g.
  {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}). You do not know fact values; never write
  a number, date, or name in place of a placeholder.
- Use only placeholders for fact ids briefed on that document.
- Do not invent people, organizations, addresses, amounts, or dates.
  People and their titles come from the briefs; the org narrative sets
  tone only.
- Every entry in a doc's `mentions` list must appear VERBATIM (the exact
  `surface` string) somewhere in that doc's text. Sigblock signers count
  as mentions of themselves. Short surfaces are nicknames: work them into
  prose naturally ("...as {{nickname}} noted..."), alongside, not instead
  of, the person's full name.
- If a doc carries `engagement_position`, honor it: it states where the
  document sits in its engagement's timeline. Do not describe progress or a
  phase inconsistent with it, and do not state the engagement's start or
  end date (those are fact placeholders, not yours to write).
- If a doc carries `firm_digest`, it is the ONLY firm history you may treat
  as established as of this document's date. Reference clients only through
  the placeholders it names; claim no engagement it does not list; present
  nothing later than this document as already true.
- If a doc carries `reporting_line`, the person reports to exactly who it
  names and to no one else. Do not name any other person or title as their
  supervisor; a reporting relationship is owned by the ledger, not invented.
- If a doc's `guidance` carries a STRUCTURE FOR THIS DOCUMENT section, that
  skeleton is binding and overrides the genre's default shape. Cover every
  numbered item, using at least the block kind it names, and use NONE of the
  block kinds it forbids anywhere in that document. Two documents of one
  genre are deliberately given different skeletons; write the one you were
  given rather than the arrangement the genre usually takes.
- Write plain, era-appropriate business prose in the org's voice.

authors.name: Robert Lawrence
authors.title: Managing Actuary
authors.persona: Robert Lawrence signs the firm's actuarial opinions and writes like someone who expects every sentence to be read back to him by a board's counsel: short, plain, and stripped of adjectives. He states the scope, the data relied on, and the standards the work was performed under before he says anything about results, and a conclusion that rests on an assumption gets its own paragraph. When he needs something from a client or a colleague he first explains in a line why it matters, then sets out what he needs as a numbered list.

participants.name: Jeffrey Ochoa
participants.title: Actuarial Analyst
participants.persona: Jeffrey Ochoa does much of the groundwork for experience studies and assumption reviews, and he is the analyst most likely to be asked how a table was built. His emails are crisp and businesslike: the finding first, then the supporting detail, then any request framed by a sentence of context about why the item is needed. He marks the difference between an observed trend and a recommended assumption every time, sometimes more insistently than a reader would like, and he skips preamble entirely.

participants.name: Amanda White
participants.title: Actuarial Associate
participants.persona: Amanda White prepares exhibits and checks the calculations that go into reports for pension boards and fund trustees. Her writing is formal and compact, short sentences in short paragraphs, and she gives a line of background before any question so the recipient does not have to hunt for the reason. She is meticulous about labeling which figures are measured from the data and which follow from an assumption, and she rarely offers an opinion of her own that has not been reviewed.

participants.name: Jennifer Vasquez
participants.title: Consulting Actuary
participants.persona: Jennifer Vasquez runs the day-to-day consulting work and is the actuary that pension staff and fund administrators hear from most often. Her writing is organized and economical, with short sentences, short paragraphs, headings that follow the order of the analysis, and a hard line between what the census data show and what the valuation assumes. She reviews analysts' work closely, marks any number she cannot trace to a source, and never asks for anything without first saying what it is for.
